\chapter{The House, and Who Is Inside It}
\label{ch:la-domus}
\hlchaptermodality{44}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the parts of a house in Latin — the building, its door, its wall, its garden and its hearth — and point to the English words each one left behind.}

The fifth word of the group, taken apart against the four before it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[domus, domūs]{domus — the building a family lives in, and the root under domestic, dome and dominate}

\label{lesson:LA-C44-domus}



\begin{quote}
A new group of five words begins here. Nothing is assumed but the alphabet you already read.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{domus} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a house}.\textquotedblright{}

Not the walls. Latin has another word for those. \textbf{Domus} is the household as a thing: the building \emph{and} the family in it, the way English \emph{house} can mean a dynasty.

Its owner is the \textbf{dominus}, the master of it — and that word travelled further than almost any other in this book. It is the \emph{don} of Spanish, the \emph{Dom} of Portuguese, and, softened through French, the \textbf{dame} and \textbf{madam} of English. A \textbf{domain} is what a \emph{dominus} holds. To \textbf{dominate} is to act like one. And a \textbf{dungeon} is the same word: French \emph{donjon}, the lord's own tower, which came to mean the cell beneath it.

The building itself gave English \textbf{domestic} and \textbf{domicile}, and — through Italian \emph{duomo}, \textquotedblleft{}the house of God\textquotedblright{} — the \textbf{dome} on top of a cathedral.

One honest note. English \textbf{home} is \emph{not} from \emph{domus}. It is Germanic, from a different root entirely. The resemblance is close enough to be tempting and it is a coincidence, and this book will always tell you when a resemblance is one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{domus, domūs}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \textbf{dominus}? (The \textbf{master of the house}.) Name two English words from him. (\textbf{Dominate}, \textbf{domain}, \textbf{dame}, \textbf{dungeon}.) And is English \emph{home} related? (\textbf{No} — Germanic, and the likeness is a coincidence.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[porta, portae]{porta — and the reason a harbour, a porch and a portal are all the same word}

\label{lesson:LA-C44-porta}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{porta} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a door},\textquotedblright{} or a \textbf{gate}.

The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*per-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to pass through,\textquotedblright{} and that is worth holding onto, because it explains a family of English words that look unrelated.

A \textbf{portal} is a \emph{porta} made grand. A \textbf{porch} is a \emph{porticus}, the covered way in front of one. And a \textbf{port} is a \emph{\textbf{portus}} — the same root again, a place where you pass through, but from the sea rather than from the street.

Rome named its gates and remembered them: the \emph{Porta Capēna}, the \emph{Porta Flāminia}. A city's gates were its addresses.

Two things to keep apart, because Latin does. \textbf{Porta} is the \emph{opening}. \textbf{Ianua} — the door leaf that swings in it — is a different word, and it is the one that named \textbf{January}, the month standing in the doorway of the year.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{porta, portae}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the root of \emph{porta} mean? (\textbf{To pass through}.) So what is a \textbf{port}? (A \textbf{way in}, from the sea.) And which Latin word for a door named a month? (\textbf{Ianua} — January.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mūrus, mūrī]{mūrus — the one that keeps things out, not the one that divides a room}

\label{lesson:LA-C44-murus}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mūrus} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a wall}.\textquotedblright{}

Latin splits what English lumps together. A \textbf{mūrus} is a wall that \textbf{defends}: the wall around a city, the wall of a fort. The wall between two rooms is a \emph{\textbf{pariēs}}, a different word altogether, and no Roman would confuse them.

English has one word for both and has to add an adjective — \emph{city wall}, \emph{interior wall}. That is a small, ordinary example of something this book will show you again and again: a language's vocabulary records what its speakers needed to tell apart.

From \emph{mūrus} English has \textbf{mural}, a painting made \emph{on} a wall, and \textbf{immure}, to shut someone inside one. The Roman wall of Britain is still called by its builder's name rather than this word — but \emph{Hadrian's Wall} is a \emph{mūrus} in every sense Latin meant.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mūrus, mūrī}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which kind of wall is a \textbf{mūrus}? (One that \textbf{defends}.) What is the other word? (\emph{\textbf{Pariēs}}, a partition.) And what is a \textbf{mural}? (A painting \textbf{on a wall}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hortus, hortī]{hortus — an enclosed piece of ground, and a true blood relative of English yard and garden}

\label{lesson:LA-C44-hortus}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hortus} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a garden}.\textquotedblright{}

This one is a \textbf{cousin, not a loan}, and that distinction is the engine of this whole book.

The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*ǵ\textsuperscript{h}órtos}}, \textquotedblleft{}an enclosure\textquotedblright{} — a piece of ground with something round it. Latin took it as \emph{hortus}. Germanic took the same word down its own road and English inherited it twice: as \textbf{yard}, the enclosed ground by a house, and — through Frankish and Old French — as \textbf{garden}. Three words, one ancestor, no borrowing between them.

The Latin form did lend as well: \textbf{horticulture} is the \emph{cultivation} of a \emph{hortus}, and it entered English from books rather than from speech, which is why it sounds bookish beside \emph{yard}.

Look at what the enclosure meant. A garden is not defined by what grows in it. It is defined by the \textbf{fence}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hortus, hortī}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is English \emph{yard} borrowed from \emph{hortus}, or descended from the same ancestor? (\textbf{Descended} — a cousin.) What did the root mean? (\textbf{An enclosure}.) And what is \textbf{horticulture}? (Cultivating a \textbf{garden}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[focus, focī]{focus — the fire in the middle of the house, and the reason a lens has a focus}

\label{lesson:LA-C44-focus}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{focus} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the hearth}.\textquotedblright{}

The fireplace. The one warm point a Roman house was arranged around — and Latin had a \emph{different} word for fire itself, which you will meet shortly.

Two roads out of this word, and they could hardly be less alike.

\textbf{The spoken road.} In late spoken Latin \emph{focus} stopped meaning the fireplace and started meaning the \textbf{fire}, the way English \emph{hearth} can. That is the word the Romance languages inherited: French \textbf{feu}, Spanish \textbf{fuego}, Italian \textbf{fuoco}, Portuguese \textbf{fogo}. None of them descends from Latin's own word for fire.

\textbf{The written road.} In 1604 Kepler needed a name for the point where a lens gathers light — the point where it would \textbf{burn} — and reached back into Latin for \emph{focus}, the burning-place. That is the \textbf{focus} English uses today, and the verb \emph{to focus} comes from it.

So the same word gives you a Spanish campfire and a camera lens, by two roads fifteen centuries apart.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{focus, focī}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{focus} mean in classical Latin? (\textbf{The hearth}.) What became of it in spoken Latin? (It came to mean \textbf{fire} — French \emph{feu}, Spanish \emph{fuego}.) And why did Kepler choose it for a lens? (Because it is the \textbf{burning-point}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
